title: Respiration
objective: After this level you can explain how cells release energy from food.
summary: Cells combine glucose with oxygen in their mitochondria, making carbon dioxide and water and capturing the energy in ATP, step by step. It's photosynthesis run in reverse.

cards.headline: Every breath out carries away a little of your breakfast.
cards.body: The carbon in the carbon dioxide you exhale was, not long ago, part of your food. How did it get from your plate to your breath?

cards.fact: Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy.
cards.context: In symbols, C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O. It happens inside your cells, in tiny compartments called mitochondria, which use oxygen and give off carbon dioxide as waste. Breathing is just the delivery service: your lungs bring the oxygen in and carry the carbon dioxide, and your breakfast's carbon, back out.

cards.headline: Photosynthesis, run backward
cards.body: Put this next to Level 75's equation. Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Respiration turns glucose and oxygen back into carbon dioxide and water. Each one's products are the other's ingredients. The plant packs the Sun's energy into sugar; your cells unpack it.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: each one's products are the other's ingredients.

cards.headline: Small change, not a bonfire
cards.body: Your cells don't release a sugar's energy all at once. They take it apart in small steps instead of a single destructive burst, capturing the energy as they go in a molecule called ATP. ATP is often called the cell's energy currency: like breaking a big bill into coins (an analogy), it lets every part of the cell pay for exactly what it needs.

cards.headline: Respiration: released
learned: Glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy
It happens mostly in the mitochondria; lungs handle delivery
Energy is released in small steps and captured in ATP

questions.prompt: What does cellular respiration produce from glucose and oxygen?

options.label: Starch and nitrogen
options.rationale: Starch is stored glucose, not a product of respiration.

questions.explanation: Glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy, mostly in the mitochondria.

questions.prompt: Why do cells break down glucose in many small steps instead of one quick burst?

options.label: To make the glucose last forever
options.rationale: The glucose is still used up; the steps are about the energy.

options.label: So they can capture the energy in ATP as it's released
Because oxygen can only react slowly
options.rationale: The steps exist so the energy can be captured, not because of oxygen.

options.label: To avoid making any carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Releasing energy in small steps lets cells capture it in ATP, the cell's energy currency, instead of losing it in one destructive burst.

questions.prompt: Level 52 says reactions never create or destroy matter. So where does the carbon in your breakfast end up?

options.label: It is destroyed to release energy
options.rationale: Reactions rearrange atoms; none are destroyed.

options.label: It turns into oxygen in your lungs
Largely in the carbon dioxide you breathe out

questions.explanation: Respiration turns glucose into carbon dioxide, and you breathe that carbon back out.
